scope: Original 50-part production hardening specification; no requirements removed or narrowed.
preamble:
You are now the Principal Production Engineer, SRE, Application Security Architect, Distributed Systems Engineer, Database Reliability Engineer, Performance Engineer and Red-Team Defensive Reviewer for the Agon eRetail / OMS / WMS / Central Inventory platform.

This task is NOT primarily about adding business features.

The business functionality is being implemented separately.

Your objective here is to make the existing application capable of operating continuously under realistic enterprise load while preserving:

* inventory correctness
* order correctness
* tenant isolation
* provider isolation
* authentication
* authorization
* transaction integrity
* queue integrity
* webhook integrity
* notification integrity
* data provenance
* recovery
* observability
* controlled latency
* controlled resource usage
* graceful degradation

The target is NOT “pretend that failures cannot happen”.

The target is:

NO SILENT CORRUPTION
NO UNSAFE RETRY
NO UNKNOWN FAILURE WITHOUT RECOVERY PATH
NO SECURITY BYPASS
NO CROSS-TENANT DATA ACCESS
NO DUPLICATE PHYSICAL STOCK MOVEMENT
NO DOUBLE RESERVATION
NO DOUBLE NOTIFICATION
NO UNBOUNDED QUEUE GROWTH
NO UNBOUNDED MEMORY GROWTH
NO CONNECTION POOL EXHAUSTION WITHOUT CONTROL
NO THREAD/WORKER STARVATION
NO UNBOUNDED PROVIDER RETRY
NO SINGLE DEPENDENCY FAILURE COLLAPSING THE WHOLE SYSTEM
NO FALSE SUCCESS

And:

BOUNDED LATENCY
BOUNDED RETRIES
BOUNDED MEMORY
BOUNDED CONNECTIONS
BOUNDED QUEUE RETENTION
BOUNDED PAYLOAD SIZE
BOUNDED JOB EXECUTION
BOUNDED CONCURRENCY
GRACEFUL DEGRADATION
AUTOMATIC RECOVERY WHERE SAFE
EXPLICIT RECONCILIATION WHERE AUTOMATIC RECOVERY IS NOT SAFE

Do not promise “zero failures”.
Engineer the system so failures are contained, visible, recoverable and incapable of silently corrupting business truth.

============================================================

parts.title: DEFINE THE NON-NEGOTIABLE SAFETY INVARIANTS
parts.originalText:
PART 2 — DEFINE THE NON-NEGOTIABLE SAFETY INVARIANTS
====================================================

The following are hard invariants.

A failed operation must never silently become success.

A timed-out operation must never automatically become “not executed”.

An external provider mutation that may already have succeeded must enter UNKNOWN_REMOTE_STATE until reconciled.

A provider observation must never overwrite Central Inventory physical truth.

A retry must never duplicate a physical stock movement.

An exact order replay must never create a second reservation.

An exact notification replay must never create a second logical notification.

A return replay must never restore physical stock twice.

A cancellation replay must never release stock twice.

A mapping update must never redirect an already-created reservation to another SKU/location.

A worker must never execute another tenant's task.

A provider account must never access another tenant.

A notification callback must never update another sender/account/tenant.

No request may cause unbounded database work.

No request may cause unbounded memory growth.

No provider may cause infinite retry loops.

No user input may become executable code.

No secret may appear in logs, URLs, responses, browser persistence or error messages.

No public endpoint may expose operational internals.

No security decision may depend only on frontend behavior.

============================================================

parts.title: PERFORMANCE / LOW-LATENCY ENGINEERING
parts.originalText:
PART 3 — PERFORMANCE / LOW-LATENCY ENGINEERING
==============================================

Do not claim “no lag”.

Instead establish measurable latency objectives.

For every critical path measure:

ORDER_INGEST
ORDER_NORMALIZATION
RESERVATION
INVENTORY_MUTATION
OUTBOX_ENQUEUE
WORKER_START
PROVIDER_REQUEST
PROVIDER_ACK
PROVIDER_READBACK
RECONCILIATION
WHATSAPP_ACCEPT
WHATSAPP_DELIVERY_CALLBACK
UI_VISIBLE_UPDATE

Measure:

p50
p95
p99
maximum observed

Do not use average latency as the primary reliability metric.

Identify:

* N+1 queries
* unnecessary provider calls
* duplicate DB reads
* repeated mapping resolution
* unbounded joins
* missing indexes
* sequential provider requests that can safely be bounded/concurrent
* synchronous work on request path
* heavy ExcelJS/XLSX processing on the main request
* expensive serialization
* large JSON payloads
* unnecessary React rerenders
* polling too aggressively
* polling too infrequently
* browser waterfalls
* duplicate API requests
* repeated dashboard refreshes
* expensive count queries
* full-table scans
* unbounded search
* offset pagination on large tables
* large report generation in request/response cycle

Critical user requests must not wait on slow providers unless the business operation truly requires synchronous provider confirmation.

Prefer:

REQUEST
→ durable local commit
→ immediate response
→ worker
→ provider
→ readback
→ UI status

where business semantics permit.

============================================================

parts.title: DATABASE PERFORMANCE

PART 4 — DATABASE PERFORMANCE

Audit every PostgreSQL query.

Identify:

* missing indexes
* wrong composite indexes
* sequential scans
* high-cardinality filters without indexes
* joins without supporting indexes
* lock contention
* long transactions
* idle-in-transaction sessions
* excessive row locking
* advisory-lock contention
* deadlock potential
* connection pool exhaustion
* oversized transactions
* unbounded result sets
* inefficient ORDER BY
* COUNT(*) on huge datasets
* unnecessary DISTINCT
* repeated lookup queries
* hot rows

Pay particular attention to:

ci_inventory_event
ci_inventory_balance
ci_reservation
ci_unified_order
ci_unified_order_line
provider accounts
provider mappings
publication tasks
notification tasks
reconciliation tables
inbox/outbox
lease tables
audit tables

For every critical query:

EXPLAIN
EXPLAIN ANALYZE where safe
index coverage
row estimates
lock behavior

Do not introduce indexes blindly.
Measure and justify them.

parts.title: CONNECTION POOLS

PART 5 — CONNECTION POOLS
=========================

Audit PostgreSQL and MongoDB connection handling.

Guarantee:

* bounded pool size
* connection timeout
* acquisition timeout
* query timeout
* idle timeout where appropriate
* clean release
* transaction cleanup
* broken connection removal
* bounded reconnect
* single-flight reconnect where appropriate
* shutdown drain
* no connection leak
* no retry storm

Test:

pool exhaustion
database outage
database restart
terminated backend
slow query
hung transaction
network failure
connection reset
recovery

Expected behavior:

readiness = unavailable when critical dependency is unavailable

liveness remains valid while process itself is healthy

requests fail fast with truthful status

no connection pool poisoning

automatic recovery where safe

parts.title: DATABASE DEADLOCK / CONCURRENCY DEFENSE
parts.originalText:
PART 6 — DATABASE DEADLOCK / CONCURRENCY DEFENSE
================================================

Identify every pair of transactions that can lock overlapping rows.

Standardize lock ordering.

Find:

* deadlock cycles
* inconsistent lock acquisition order
* row hot spots
* long-held locks
* transaction work performed while external network requests are pending

NEVER hold an important database transaction open while waiting indefinitely for a provider API.

Provider calls should generally occur outside the database transaction unless the design explicitly requires otherwise.

Where remote operations interact with local state, use:

outbox
idempotency
state machine
readback
reconciliation

rather than pretending to have distributed ACID.

============================================================

parts.title: PROVIDER SECURITY
parts.originalText:
PART 10 — PROVIDER SECURITY
===========================

For every provider call:

* validate account ownership
* validate tenant
* use stored credential
* enforce allowed destination
* prevent SSRF
* prevent DNS rebinding
* prevent internal-network access
* require TLS
* bound connection timeout
* bound response timeout
* bound response size
* classify errors
* redact secrets

Never allow arbitrary user-supplied URLs.

Never disable certificate verification.

Never log Authorization headers.

Never log access tokens.

Never log webhook secrets.

Never expose provider credential material to frontend clients.

============================================================

parts.title: RATE LIMIT / RETRY CONTROL
parts.originalText:
PART 13 — RATE LIMIT / RETRY CONTROL
====================================

Build provider-specific retry classification.

Retry only when safe.

Retryable:

transient network failure
provider 429
selected temporary 5xx
connection reset

Not automatically retryable:

authentication failure
authorization failure
validation failure
permanent 4xx
unknown mutation outcome

Unknown mutation outcome:

UNKNOWN_REMOTE_STATE
→ reconcile/readback
→ only then decide next action

Implement:

exponential backoff
jitter
retry cap
account-level pacing
circuit breaker
dead-letter

Avoid synchronized retry storms.

Test large simultaneous failures.

============================================================

parts.title: CASCADING FAILURE CONTROL
parts.originalText:
PART 14 — CASCADING FAILURE CONTROL
===================================

Assume a marketplace provider is unavailable for 30 minutes.

The system must NOT:

* block web requests
* exhaust worker threads
* exhaust DB connections
* retry infinitely
* fill memory with pending objects
* generate millions of duplicate tasks
* spam WhatsApp
* mark orders successful incorrectly
* mark stock reconciled
* collapse unrelated providers

Provider A failure must not bring down:

Provider B
Central Inventory reads
local order search
admin UI
other queues
authentication
health endpoints

Use isolation:

provider/account concurrency limits
bounded queues
separate worker pools where justified
circuit breakers
backpressure
dead-letter
rate limiting

============================================================

parts.title: ORDER/INVENTORY SAFETY

PART 17 — ORDER/INVENTORY SAFETY
================================

Simulate multiple marketplaces selling the same SKU.

Example:

Opening stock = 10

Shopify order = 6
Flipkart order = 5
Amazon order = 4

Send simultaneously.

The system must guarantee that committed reservations cannot exceed sellable stock.

Do not solve by trusting application-level “check first”.

Use database transactional correctness.

Repeat with:

* two locations
* pack size
* same order replay
* webhook/poll overlap
* cancellation race
* dispatch race
* return race

parts.title: INVENTORY PUBLICATION SAFETY
parts.originalText:
PART 18 — INVENTORY PUBLICATION SAFETY
======================================

For every provider inventory mutation:

expected local quantity
→ publication identity
→ provider request
→ provider result
→ readback
→ reconciliation

If request times out:

do NOT blindly resend.

If provider was potentially successful:

UNKNOWN_REMOTE_STATE

Read provider.

Match:
RECONCILED

Mismatch:
REQUIRES_RECONCILIATION

This is mandatory.

PART 37 — PERFORMANCE ANTI-PATTERNS
===================================

Search specifically for:

await inside large loops
sequential provider calls
unbounded Promise.all
Promise.all over unbounded database results
large arrays
recursive retry

unbounded event listeners
unbounded queue insertion

PART 41 — NO-COLLAPSE PRINCIPLE
===============================

The platform must degrade by capability, not collapse globally.

Example:

Flipkart unavailable:

Flipkart:
DEGRADED

Shopify:
HEALTHY

Central Inventory:
HEALTHY

Amazon:
HEALTHY

WhatsApp:
HEALTHY

The entire application must not become unavailable merely because one provider is down.

Similarly:

WhatsApp unavailable
≠
orders unavailable.

Provider inventory readback unavailable
≠
Central Inventory corrupted.

Mongo legacy unavailable
≠
PostgreSQL Central Inventory unavailable.

Use dependency isolation.

parts.title: FINAL ENGINEERING QUESTION
parts.originalText:
PART 50 — FINAL ENGINEERING QUESTION
====================================

At the end, answer this:

Can Agon continue operating safely when:

* one marketplace is unavailable?
* multiple marketplaces fail simultaneously?
* provider response latency increases 20x?
* provider returns 429 for 20 minutes?
* database connections are exhausted?
* one worker crashes?
* two workers race?
* webhook delivery is duplicated?
* webhook delivery is missing?
* polling overlaps webhook?
* provider accepts a mutation but the response is lost?
* provider readback disagrees?
* WhatsApp goes down?
* Mongo goes down?
* PostgreSQL becomes slow?
* a large Excel workbook is uploaded?
* a malicious file is uploaded?
* an attacker changes tenant IDs?
* an attacker changes object IDs?
* a session expires during a mutation?
* a user double-clicks a destructive action?
* deployment restarts during processing?
* database restore occurs?
* queue backlog becomes very large?

For each answer provide:

EXPECTED
CURRENT
EVIDENCE
REMAINING RISK
RECOMMENDED CONTROL

Final requirement:

Do not claim that the system cannot fail.

Prove that failures are:
DETECTED
BOUNDED
ISOLATED
AUDITABLE
RECOVERABLE
OR EXPLICITLY RECONCILABLE

The production objective is:

A failure may interrupt a capability.

A failure must NOT silently corrupt business truth.

A security attack may be rejected.

A provider may become unavailable.

A worker may crash.

A network may fail.

A database may restart.

But the platform must preserve:
inventory integrity
order integrity
tenant isolation
auditability
recovery
and truthful operator state.
